name: ACMG five-category CNV pathogenicity classification against expert labels (Zhang et al. Table 3)
description: Run each tool on the 3,031 CNVs and compare its five-category output (benign, likely benign, VUS, likely pathogenic, pathogenic) with the expert classification; report accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, FPR, F1 and MCC.

attributes.protocol: Run each tool on the 3,031 CNVs and compare its five-category output (benign, likely benign, VUS, likely pathogenic, pathogenic) with the expert classification; report accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, FPR, F1 and MCC.
attributes.source_locator: Table 3; Methods 'Data analysis'; Results 'Comparative analysis of clinical metrics'
limitations: How the five-class metrics are averaged across classes is not stated.
Reference labels are expert ACMG classifications, a semi-quantitative standard with known inter-reviewer variability (Discussion paragraph 5).
The set is enriched for pregnancy-loss and prenatal cases and is imbalanced (benign is about half of the duplications), which the authors say affects the metrics (Discussion paragraphs 5 and 6).
Classification of already detected CNVs from their coordinates; no read data or detection step is evaluated.
Some training sets of the evaluated tools (ClinVar, ClinGen, DGV) may overlap the published cohorts used as reference; the paper does not test this.

Two of the three authors (X. Zhang and D. Chen) are authors of dbCNV (reference 24), developed in the same laboratory, so the dbCNV rows are author_reported. dbCNV's original test set was that laboratory's internal dataset, and this benchmark includes the laboratory's internal CNV-seq cases (December 2019 to November 2025); overlap is not tested. The paper declares no competing interests.

Supplementary Table S1 (MarCNV-ISV conservative and progressive modes) was not retrieved.
The benchmark dataset is not public ('available from the corresponding author on reasonable request').
Not archived in the batch: CC BY-NC-ND licence; hash and locators only.
The Abstract gives ClassifyCNV VUS accuracy 95.33%; Table 4 prints 94.92% (duplications) and 95.74% (deletions), which with the Table 2 class sizes (886 and 329) pool to about 95.1%.
Two Table 4 deletion cells are not a whole-number share of the Table 2 class size (AnnotSV P 95.16% of 287 P and LP deletions; MarCNV-ISV VUS 89.86% of 329 VUS deletions); the other 28 cells are.

name: Relevance of ACMG five-category CNV pathogenicity classification against expert labels (Zhang et al. Table 3) to "Select a copy-number variant detection and characterisation workflow"
description: Proxy: automated pathogenicity classification of already detected CNVs bears on the characterisation and analyst-assessment part of the question, but no detection from sequencing reads is evaluated and the reference is expert ACMG labelling.

attributes.endpoint: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, FPR, F1 and MCC of AnnotSV, ClassifyCNV, dbCNV, MarCNV-ISV and X-CNV against expert ACMG classifications
attributes.rationale: Proxy: automated pathogenicity classification of already detected CNVs bears on the characterisation and analyst-assessment part of the question, but no detection from sequencing reads is evaluated and the reference is expert ACMG labelling.
constraints: Inspect every linked evaluation's source locator before citing a result.
Do not combine this mapping's evaluations with detection results from other protocols; the endpoint is classification, not detection.
limitations: How the five-class metrics are averaged across classes is not stated.
Reference labels are expert ACMG classifications, a semi-quantitative standard with known inter-reviewer variability (Discussion paragraph 5).
The set is enriched for pregnancy-loss and prenatal cases and is imbalanced (benign is about half of the duplications), which the authors say affects the metrics (Discussion paragraphs 5 and 6).
Classification of already detected CNVs from their coordinates; no read data or detection step is evaluated.
Some training sets of the evaluated tools (ClinVar, ClinGen, DGV) may overlap the published cohorts used as reference; the paper does not test this.

Two of the three authors (X. Zhang and D. Chen) are authors of dbCNV (reference 24), developed in the same laboratory, so the dbCNV rows are author_reported. dbCNV's original test set was that laboratory's internal dataset, and this benchmark includes the laboratory's internal CNV-seq cases (December 2019 to November 2025); overlap is not tested. The paper declares no competing interests.
